solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unexpected repayment plus an additional sum?

definitions.note: noun sense: an extra amount paid on top

indicators.note: something unexpected turns out differently, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A surprise refund arrives as a bonus on top of what was owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unexpected' rearranges REPAYMENT PLUS; the question mark admits that the adjective is being stretched to stand for an extra payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Something supplementary is added to complete or extend, so an extra payment fits that description.

clue.text: Very good person that is hugging little darling

indicators.note: one piece wraps round another as arms enclose a body

parts.note: a saint, abbreviated ST
wee is Scottish for small
IE abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A kindly person embraces a small sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hugging' is the container signal; the saint is the crossword's usual very good person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are affectionate terms of address for a loved one, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Scrape ice off animals

indicators.note: off as in gone bad or out of order, so these letters are spoiled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An instruction to clear frost from some creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like part of the phrase 'scrape off' but it is the anagram signal for SCRAPE ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Peccaries are pig-like hoofed mammals of the Americas, so they are an example of animals.

clue.text: From what we hear, toilet fastener is something flowery

indicators.note: signals that the spoken form of the words, not their spelling, gives the letters

parts.note: loo is everyday British slang for a lavatory; a pin fastens things together

explanation.surface: A lavatory latch is apparently decorative.
explanation.walkthrough: LOO is everyday British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A lupin is a garden plant grown for its tall spikes of blooms, so it is something with flowers.

clue.text: Mottled appearance to have a bad effect on glitzy stuff

parts.words: to have a bad effect on
parts.note: to mar is to spoil or damage
bling is flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: A blotchy look spoils the shine of flashy jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: Marbling is a streaky pattern like that of marble, a kind of mottled look.

clue.text: Spooky things when most people are asleep?

indicators.note: spooky as in weird and unsettled, so the letters of the next word are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: Ghostly goings-on that happen while everyone sleeps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooky' looks like a description of ghosts but signals the rearrangement of THINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark hours after evening are the usual sleeping time, hence the question mark for a description rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Aggressive type bringing trouble to worker, idiot at the top

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece at the top comes first

parts.note: an ass is a fool
to ail is to trouble or afflict
a worker ant, the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: An aggressive person torments a labourer, with a fool in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the top' places ASS first in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An assailant is an attacker, a person who behaves aggressively towards someone.

clue.text: No guy is properly developed in early life

indicators.note: developed as in worked into a new form, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: No man matures fully while still a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'properly developed' rearranges NO GUY.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone young is at an early stage of life, so the phrase describes the adjective's sense.

clue.text: Tune running moderately with speed dropped

indicators.note: running as in flowing loosely, so the remaining letters are rearranged
dropped means taken out of the word

parts.note: rate is speed

explanation.surface: A musical direction: play at a moderate pace, not fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped' removes RATE from MODERATELY to leave MODELY, which 'running' rearranges. The surface reads like a tempo marking.
explanation.definitionFit: A melody is an air or tune, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: One getting away from English society with a leap

parts.note: a caper is a playful leap

explanation.surface: Someone fleeing English high society in a single bound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' looks like it goes with 'getting away' but is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An escaper is someone who breaks free, one who gets away.

clue.text: Sign gets a bit mangled by river

indicators.note: slightly crushed out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England

explanation.surface: A notice gets damaged by a riverside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit mangled' rearranges GETS to GEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A gesture is a movement made as a signal, so it is a kind of sign.

clue.text: Coach? Yes and no

parts.note: to coach is to instruct, so yes; but a railway coach is only one carriage of the whole, so no

explanation.surface: A teasing question about whether something counts as a coach.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense agrees with 'Coach'; the railway sense disagrees, since a coach is merely a carriage within it.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to instruct or drill; as a noun it is a line of carriages, of which a coach is just one.

clue.text: Releasing accommodation to rent, given sign to proceed

parts.note: a letting is a property rented out
go is the signal to move on, as on a traffic light

explanation.surface: Rental housing is released once the go-ahead is given.
explanation.definitionFit: To let go is to release one's hold, so the participle phrase means freeing.

clue.text: Current range is being restricted

indicators.note: a word that is restricted is held in by another, so it sits inside

parts.note: an extent is the range or scope of something

explanation.surface: The present range of something is under limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being restricted' is the container signal. 'Current' looks like electricity or water but means existing now.
explanation.definitionFit: Something existent is in being now, which is what current means as an adjective.

clue.text: Examiner has sealed lip in academic period

indicators.note: to seal something in is to close it inside, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a tester examines things
a rim is a lip or edge

explanation.surface: An invigilator keeps quiet during the term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has sealed' is the container signal; 'sealed lip' suggests keeping silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimester is one of three terms in some universities' year, a period of study.

clue.text: Disparity that may not be heard?

definitions.meaning: a great difference, as in one thing being very unlike another
a shout from a long distance away might not reach the listener

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the idiom literally as a shout made a long way off.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means something very different from another; taken literally, it is a shout from far away.

clue.text: Beat restricting America, one opposing sense, finally producing an effect?

indicators.note: a word restricting another holds it in, so one sits inside the other

parts.note: to cat is an old verb meaning to flog with a cat-o'-nine-tails
USA abbreviates the United States of America
I is the Roman numeral one
V abbreviates versus, opposing

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word sense

explanation.surface: Whipping hemmed in America, one critic of reason ultimately getting results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restricting' is the container signal and 'finally' takes the last letter of sense. To cat is an old verb for flogging with a cat-o'-nine-tails.
explanation.definitionFit: Causative describes what brings about a result, so it means making something happen.

clue.text: Naughty harlot I love, being a womaniser

indicators.note: naughty as in misbehaving, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A man confesses his affection for a wicked woman, showing he chases women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naughty' rearranges HARLOT I; 'being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lothario, after a seducer in an 18th-century play, is a man who seduces women.

clue.text: The fellow's holy daughter is hairy

parts.note: his means belonging to the man
pi is slang for pious

explanation.surface: A man's devout daughter is described as hairy.
explanation.walkthrough: PI is old British school slang for pious or sanctimonious.
explanation.definitionFit: Hispid is a botanical and zoological term for covered in stiff bristles, so it means shaggy.

clue.text: The drunk grabbing copper, a cool dude?

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece goes round the other
drunk as in reeling, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: PC is a police constable, a copper in British slang

explanation.surface: The drunkard seizes a policeman; is he a hipster?
explanation.walkthrough: Copper looks like the metal Cu but is a British police officer, a PC; the drunk letters are HET.
explanation.definitionFit: A hepcat is old jazz-age slang for a hip, stylish person, much as cool dude is.

clue.text: Little fellow and two maidens randomly entering bubbly hot tub

indicators.note: the maidens go in at random, and bubbly suggests a churning jacuzzi, so all the letters are mixed

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for maiden over, so two give MM

explanation.surface: A small man and two young women climb into a fizzing jacuzzi.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase 'randomly entering bubbly' signals the mixing of the two maidens with HOT TUB; M is the cricket abbreviation for maiden over.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Thumb is the folk-tale hero no bigger than a thumb, so he is a tiny man.

clue.text: Spooner's to set down meat and herb

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two starts change places

parts.note: to lay is to put down
beef is meat

explanation.surface: A recipe step: put down the meat and the herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' swaps the opening sounds; the second word is respelt after the swap, so the change is by ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaf of the sweet bay tree is used to flavour stews, so it is an example of a herb.

clue.text: Church in square in old town where creed was settled

definitions.text: old town where creed was settled
definitions.note: adjective use: of Nicaea, the ancient town where the Christian creed was agreed in 325

indicators.note: one piece put in another sits inside it

parts.note: nine is a square number, three times three
CE abbreviates Church of England

explanation.surface: A church in a town square where a statement of faith was agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square' looks like a town square but is the number nine. The definition names the town, and the answer is its adjective, as in the Nicene Creed.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective refers to Nicaea, the ancient city whose council in 325 fixed the Christian statement of belief.

clue.text: Pompous nonsense about eg owl beginning to fly off

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: pish is an exclamation of contempt meaning nonsense

indicators.note: the first letter departs, as a bird flies away

parts.note: a hooter is something that hoots, such as an owl

explanation.surface: Someone is pompous and talks rubbish about birds that fly away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to fly off' drops the first letter of the owl word, and 'about' is the container signal. Mr Pooter is the self-important narrator of The Diary of a Nobody.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from Mr Pooter, a self-important suburban clerk, so it means fussily pompous.

clue.text: Unsteady love no female repeatedly wanted

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: repeatedly means the letter appears twice

explanation.surface: A shaky romance: no woman wanted again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanted' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on-off is intermittent, starting and stopping, so not steady.

clue.text: Clothes by end of stairway — ready for bed?

parts.note: wear is clothing, as in menswear

indicators.note: the end of the word stairway is its last letter

explanation.surface: Pyjamas left at the top of the stairs for bedtime.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tired means needing sleep, so the question mark allows the indirect sense of sleepy.

clue.text: Report of something that's narrow? We don't want it

indicators.note: a report is something said aloud, so the spoken form gives the letters

parts.note: a waist is the narrow middle of the body

explanation.surface: A slim figure is mentioned, and no one wants it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a news item but signals the spoken word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish and refuse are things discarded as unwanted, so the definition describes them.

clue.text: A station by which is seen the French preacher

parts.note: a post is a station or position
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A French preacher is spotted at a station.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is one sent out to spread a faith, so a missionary preacher.

clue.text: After lay-off from acting I have to be uneasy

indicators.note: after means the second piece follows the first

parts.note: an actor between jobs is said to be resting
I've, written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: An actor out of work feels uneasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the contraction second; resting is British theatre jargon for being unemployed.
explanation.definitionFit: Restive means fidgety and unable to settle, so it describes being uneasy.

clue.text: Ere long set off to get drunk and lose all inhibitions?

indicators.note: drunk as in reeling, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Soon go out to drink and let go entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get drunk' rearranges ERE LONG SET OFF.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to act out of character, abandoning normal restraint.
